## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\resizebox{0.92\linewidth}{!}{\mlphysicalstackfull{100}{20}{20}{20}{20}}
\end{marginfigure}
:::

_Why can a robot recognize what to do yet still be too late to act?_

A robot reaching for an unfamiliar mug must infer where to grasp while the mug and the surrounding world keep moving. Learned models extend the machine's ability to interpret such scenes, but a useful answer can arrive after the physical conditions that justified it have changed. Larger models also demand more memory traffic and computation from an onboard processor that must share resources with sensing and control. Predicting a sequence of future motions can keep the arm supplied between model updates, yet it cannot make those motions respond to observations the model has not received. The engineering task is to match learned capability to the time available for fresh decisions while preserving independent control of the body. Because motion beyond the causal boundary cannot be recalled, a learned proposal must remain subject to timely physical permission.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Compare classical analytical pipelines and learned representations on coverage, sensory robustness, and formal verifiability
- Calculate the memory wall bound on a model's fresh-evaluation rate ($f \le B_{\text{mem}} / M_{\text{weights}}$) under the embodied batch size 1 constraint
- Estimate key-value cache expansion from multi-camera tokenization, hidden dimensions, and retained history windows
- Explain how action chunking ($H$) amortizes off-chip weight transfers over physical wall-clock time without improving closed-loop reaction latency
- Compare action-head working sets with available cache capacity before assuming refinement avoids off-chip transfers
- Apply replanning period, inference latency, and target drift to size an action chunk for a dynamic target
- Diagnose cognitive failure modes: semantic hallucinations, uncalibrated softmax overconfidence, perceptual chattering, and expired intent leases
- Identify the trajectory, timestamps, and validity information a proposer must hand to independent real-time verification

:::

## The Embodied Brain {#sec-brain-embodied}

The warehouse mobile manipulator can stay within the torque, thermal, voltage, and stopping limits established in @sec-body and still fail to grasp an unfamiliar ceramic mug from a moving conveyor. Those limits describe what the body can sustain. They do not identify the mug's handle or choose a path around a coworker's hand. A learned model can supply that missing interpretation, but the model's output remains a candidate action until the permission path checks it against current evidence and physical limits.

The timing problem begins while the model computes. The mug keeps moving, and the arm still needs feedback to track the motion already admitted. A larger model may improve recognition while taking longer to produce the next proposal. The relevant engineering quantities are therefore distinct: how often the model incorporates a fresh observation, how many future setpoints each proposal contains, and how long its evidence remains useful. Increasing the number of setpoints does not renew the evidence behind them.

The resulting **two-speed brain architecture**\index{Two-speed brain architecture!hybrid control} separates learned deliberation from the real-time permission and tracking path (@fig-two-speed-brain). The Brain proposes a goal or a trajectory; faster control continues below the proposal boundary even when deliberation pauses. Action Chunking Transformers (ACT) [@zhao2023learning] and Diffusion Policies [@chi2024diffusionpolicy] can supply multiple future setpoints in one proposal. The permission path determines which part may execute and when continued execution must end. This division gives learning room to improve task capability without giving an inference delay authority to suspend physical protection.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/spa_locator_p.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="S·P·A locator triad with the Plan node highlighted."}

*The Plan axis: high-capacity neural deliberation emitting unprivileged action chunks.*
:::

::: {#fig-two-speed-brain fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Two-speed brain architecture**: An unprivileged deliberative realm running at $1\text{--}50\text{ Hz}$ and a real-time realm running at $1000\text{ Hz}$, separated by the proposal-permission privilege boundary. The independent safety enforcer checks sensed state and modeled limits on each control cycle before granting execution permission; a refusal path feeds state resynchronization back to the deliberative policy." fig-alt="Two-speed brain architecture showing unprivileged deliberative planning at 1 to 50 hertz crossing the proposal-permission privilege boundary to 1000 hertz real-time safety enforcement with refusal feedback."}
![](images/svg/fig03_two_speed_brain.svg){width="90%"}

A learned proposer earns its place when training gives it useful coverage beyond the hand-authored cases. For the conveyor pick, that means relating the instruction to the visible mug and proposing a graspable region. Recognition still needs measured geometry before it can specify a reachable pose, and robustness to glare or occlusion depends on the operating conditions represented in the evidence. The added capability must fit the processor and the time available to act.

@Fig-cadence-gap places these workloads beside the rates of physical control. Its points represent different workload regimes, so they do not establish a scaling law from parameter count alone. The design decision is which computation can finish before the current proposal expires; the memory and timing calculations below make that decision concrete for the mobile manipulator.

::: {#fig-cadence-gap fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Cadence regimes**: Parameter counts and example update rates for different control, vision, and embodied workloads. The points are illustrative workload regimes rather than runs on a common device, and parameter count alone does not determine update rate." fig-alt="Log-log scatter of parameter counts and example update rates for different workload classes, with shaded control and deliberation rate bands."}

@Sec-brain-classical-wall shows why pipelines built on hand-authored geometry and state machines lose coverage outside the factory cell, and @sec-brain-learned-representations shows what learned representations recover and what they cost in tokens and memory traffic. @Sec-brain-cognitive-pipeline turns that cost into the machine's numbers: the memory wall that bounds how often its intent model can run, the action chunking that keeps the arm supplied between evaluations, and the drift that bounds how long each chunk stays true. @Sec-brain-cognitive-vulnerabilities then takes up the ways a proposal can arrive on time and still be wrong, each of which leaves the permission path with a proposal it must be able to refuse.

## The Classical Wall {#sec-brain-classical-wall}

A gripper in a fixed workcell can approach the same fixture along the same path on every cycle. Engineers can describe that task through geometry, equations of motion, and explicit transitions between stages. Classical control and robotics build on this analytical approach [@wiener1948cybernetics; @kalman1960new; @craig2005introduction]. The difficulty for the conveyor mug is extending the description to objects and conditions that the engineer did not enumerate.

Analytical kinematics and dynamics map desired end-effector[^fn-hw-end-effector] motion into joint motion and actuator torque.[^fn-math-classical-dynamics] Perception can match measured geometry against a known computer-aided design (CAD) model, while a state machine advances through approaching, aligning, grasping, and retracting. In a calibrated workcell these components solve a bounded task with explicit assumptions. Their computational cost and timing still depend on the chosen algorithm, processor, and contact model.

[^fn-hw-end-effector]: **End-Effector**\index{End-effector!definition}: The active tool, gripper, or hand at the distal tip of a robotic manipulator that interacts directly with physical workpieces and the environment.

[^fn-math-classical-dynamics]: **Rigid-Body Dynamics Formulation**\index{Rigid-body dynamics!Euler-Lagrange formulation}\index{Equations of motion!manipulator dynamics}: Classical control computes generalized torques via the standard manipulator equation $\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{q}, \dot{\mathbf{q}})\dot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{q}) = \boldsymbol{\tau}$, where $\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{q})$ represents the configuration-dependent inertia matrix, $\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{q}, \dot{\mathbf{q}})$ captures Coriolis and centripetal terms, and $\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{q})$ accounts for gravitational loading. Specifically, $\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{q})$ captures configuration-dependent mass moments: extending an articulated linkage shifts mass outward from the rotational axes, increasing reflected rotational inertia ($I \propto m r^2$) and demanding quadratically higher joint torque for equivalent angular acceleration. This analytical formulation becomes computationally intractable and physically inaccurate when machines interact with unmodeled frictional contacts, fluid drag, or deformable objects. Derivations are provided in @sec-appendix-control.

::: {#fig-industrial-welding fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Industrial spot-welding workcell**: Multiple six-degree-of-freedom articulated robots execute preprogrammed spot welding paths on stamped automotive chassis at the BMW Leipzig plant. Operating in a calibrated factory environment with submillimeter repeatable fixtures and safety interlock cages, classical controllers provide deterministic cycle timing and formal stability proofs. (Credit: BMW Group / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0 de)." fig-alt="Articulated industrial robots executing automated spot welding on an automotive chassis within a safety-caged factory cell."}
![](images/jpg/fig03_real_industrial_welding.jpg){width="85%"}
:::

Where the operational environment is strictly structured and bounded (@fig-industrial-welding), classical methods provide dependable behavior within their modeled conditions. On an automated automotive assembly line, an industrial robot welds stamped steel panels where every workpiece arrives at an exact coordinate within sub-millimeter tolerances. Ambient lighting is tightly regulated by industrial fixtures, and human workers are excluded by physical interlock safety fences. Within the causal boundary defined in @sec-boundary-causal-boundary, this controlled regime permits explicit models, bounded servo timing, and formal Lyapunov stability analysis under stated assumptions. Engineers can verify trajectory tracking error bounds ($\lVert \mathbf{e}(t) \rVert \le \epsilon$) and certify controller software coverage against safety standards without collecting empirical demonstrations.

Yet when an embodied machine leaves the structured factory cage to operate in unstructured open-world environments (@fig-unstructured-rescue), this analytical paradigm hits the **classical wall** [@brooks1991intelligence; @levine2018learning]. The physical world is not a sterile CAD drawing; it is continuous, deformable, and endlessly variable.

::: {#fig-unstructured-rescue fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Unstructured search-and-rescue robot**: A tracked mobile robot navigates an obstacle course with irregular inclines, loose debris, and visual occlusions. In such unmapped environments, preauthored geometric models and rigid state machines can lose coverage; learned policies may help infer spatial affordances and traversability from sensory streams. (Credit: TU Darmstadt Rescue Robotics / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0)." fig-alt="Tracked mobile robot traversing irregular rubble and wooden obstacles in an unstructured search-and-rescue test arena."}
![](images/jpg/fig03_real_unstructured_rescue.jpg){width="85%"}
:::

Outside that workcell, the same pipeline must cope with object variation, imperfect sensing, and unexpected task states. A CAD template does not cover every deformation of a garment; glare can erase the depth edge separating two packages; and an unexpected hand can invalidate a preauthored transition from approach to grasp. Adding templates, thresholds, and branches extends coverage, but each addition requires engineering and validation for the new conditions.

Learning offers a different way to obtain that coverage. Training can associate varied observations with useful object features and demonstrated behavior without requiring a separate geometric template for every instance. This does not replace the analytical controller that tracks a proposed motion. It adds a computationally demanding interpretation stage whose memory traffic and latency must fit above that controller.

## Learned Representations {#sec-brain-learned-representations}

Asked to take the unfamiliar ceramic mug from the conveyor, a learned model can relate the instruction to a visible handle and propose a grasp region without an exact CAD template. Vision-language-action (VLA) models combine images, language, and robot state to produce candidate actions [@driess2023palme; @brohan2023rt1; @brohan2023rt2; @kim2024openvla]. Their value is the coverage obtained from training across objects and conditions, rather than a guarantee that any unfamiliar scene will be interpreted correctly.

Demonstrations can also teach coordinated behavior for tasks whose contacts and deformations are difficult to specify completely, such as routing a cable with two arms (@fig-aloha-manipulator) [@zhao2023learning; @chi2024diffusionpolicy]. Learned sensory features may tolerate variations represented in that training, while a controller still needs measured geometry and physical limits to execute the proposal. Task success under tested conditions supplies evidence of capability; it does not establish behavior under every lighting change, contact, or payload.

The systems cost follows from how that capability is represented. Images become model inputs, retained context occupies memory, and the model must compute a new action before its observations become stale. The useful comparison with a classical pipeline therefore includes both task coverage and the cost of renewing a proposal.

::: {#fig-vla-architecture fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Embodied Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architecture**: A representative dataflow. (1) Camera patches receive 2D image-position and camera identifiers alongside language and robot-state tokens; metric depth still requires calibrated evidence. (2) Self-attention mixes the combined token sequence; the colored grid illustrates internal attention weights, not a verified affordance or grasp pose. (3) Discrete autoregressive decoders emit tokens sequentially, whereas continuous decoders generate candidate multi-step chunks ($\mathbf{A}_{t:t+H-1}$) through one pass or iterative denoising. (4) An independent permission path checks candidate motion against sensed state and modeled limits before actuation. (Synthesized from Brohan et al. [@brohan2023rt1; @brohan2023rt2], Kim et al. [@kim2024openvla], and Octo Model Team [@octo_2023])." fig-alt="Comprehensive architectural schematic of a Vision-Language-Action foundation model showing spatial patch slicing, 2D positional embeddings, multimodal self-attention weights in an illustrative image grid, discrete vs. continuous action decoders, and an independent proposal boundary."}
![](images/svg/fig03_vla_architecture.svg){width="100%"}
:::

For the mug pick, the model must turn images and instructions into a candidate motion. The dataflow in @fig-vla-taxonomy and @fig-vla-architecture separates that computation into input encoding, a shared representation, and an action decoder, followed by the handoff to independent permission. A token is a vector representing part of an input, such as an image patch; the backbone combines those vectors, and the decoder turns the combined representation into proposed actions. The engineering comparison below follows what each stage stores, transfers, and delivers:

1. **Sensory Ingestion and Spatial Tokenization (The Inputs):**
   A ViT frontend slices each incoming camera frame into a grid of non-overlapping pixel patches of size $P \times P$ (typically $14 \times 14$ or $16 \times 16$ pixels). Each patch is linearly projected into a vector of width $d$, augmented with 2D spatial sinusoidal positional embeddings, and tagged with a learned camera identifier.

   On a mobile manipulator equipped with three synchronized cameras (e.g., left wrist, right wrist, and an overhead torso mount) capturing $224 \times 224$ images, the image frontend prepares a buffer for each view. Each frame yields $(224 / 14)^2 = 256$ spatial patches. Across three cameras, ingestion injects $3 \times 256 = 768$ visual tokens into the model's sequence on every perceptual step. When concatenated with tokenized natural language commands ($\sim 32$ tokens) and proprioceptive joint state embeddings ($\sim 16$ tokens), the initial context sequence length exceeds $S \approx 800$ tokens. In FP16 precision ($2\,\text{bytes}$ per element) with hidden dimension $d = 4096$, the initial token embedding matrix alone occupies:
   $$M_{\text{embed}} = S \times d \times 2\,\text{bytes} = 800 \times 4096 \times 2 \approx 6.55\,\text{MB}$$
   Crucially, 2D image coordinates and internal attention patterns do not constitute metric depth: projecting an end-effector into physical 3D space requires calibrated extrinsic camera matrices and depth telemetry.

2. **Multimodal Alignment and Attention (The Backbone):**
   The token sequence passes through $L = 32$ transformer layers where multi-head self-attention computes pairwise token interactions. While full self-attention incurs quadratic computational complexity ($O(S^2 d)$ FLOPs), at the systems level the Key-Value (KV) cache that retains prior token states for autoregressive context expands linearly ($O(L \cdot S \cdot d)$):
   $$M_{\text{KV}} = 2 \times L \times d \times S \times \text{bytes}$$
   For a 32-layer model with $d = 4096$ using FP16 storage, each context token claims $2 \times 32 \times 4096 \times 2 = 524{,}288\,\text{bytes} \approx 0.524\,\text{MB}$ of KV cache. Reading this KV cache across off-chip DRAM on every token step creates massive memory bus traffic that directly competes with weight streaming. Because memory bus access under Unified Memory Architecture (UMA) is a shared zero-sum resource, fetching tens of megabytes of KV state per step risks starving real-time sensor DMA buffers. Embodied architectures therefore deploy Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) or cross-attention decoders to compress KV-cache memory traffic by a factor of 4 to 8. Furthermore, strong attention weights between language tokens (such as "mug handle") and visual patches do not prove geometric affordance or collision-free clearance; nor does the KV cache track object permanence during physical occlusions. The formal patch-embedding, position-encoding, and attention formulations appear in @sec-appendix-ml-patch-embedding.

3. **Specialized Action Decoders (The Outputs):**
   Instead of generating open-ended conversational text, the final hidden representation $\mathbf{h}_{\text{context}} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is routed to specialized action decoders. While vision-language navigation (VLN) models emit topological waypoints or heading rates $(v_t, \omega_t)$ (@fig-vln-navigation), manipulation (VLA) models diverge sharply in how they bridge semantic representations to physical motion:

   Discrete action decoders map each action dimension to a categorical token [@brohan2023rt1; @brohan2023rt2; @kim2024openvla]. Sequential token generation can require several model evaluations for one action vector, and discretization limits spatial resolution. Continuous decoders instead emit a trajectory chunk, either directly or through iterative refinement [@chi2024diffusionpolicy; @octo_2023; @black2024pi0]:
   $$\mathbf{A}_{t:t+H-1} = [\mathbf{a}_t, \mathbf{a}_{t+1}, \dots, \mathbf{a}_{t+H-1}] \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times d_a} \quad (H = 16\text{--}64\text{ steps})$$
   Here $H$ counts future setpoints and $d_a$ counts values per action. A chunk supplies several requested motions from one sensory context; it does not contain new observations. The runtime comparison therefore depends on how many backbone and decoder evaluations produce the chunk, and how long those evaluations take. @Sec-appendix-ml-multimodal derives discrete tokenization and explains how generative decoders represent alternative demonstrated routes without averaging them into an obstacle.

4. **The Proposal Boundary (Isolation from Actuators):**
   Whether the model is a VLN mobility planner or a VLA manipulation policy, its output is a candidate proposal ($p_t$) on the unprivileged side of the proposal boundary (\ref{dfn-boundary-proposal-boundary}).\index{Unprivileged proposal!proposal boundary} Under the machine model of @sec-boundary-machine-model, the foundation model runs in user space on the application processor and has no path to the pulse-width modulation (PWM) registers or to the current in the motor coils.

   The Brain hands over candidate motion together with the time of the observations that support it. Faster downstream loops track admitted setpoints and regulate motor current using current measurements. A long neural inference cannot suspend those loops or renew old evidence. The full latency budget in @sec-brain-memory-wall prices the path from sensing to actuation; @sec-nervous-invariant-checking develops the independent checking responsibility.

::: {#dfn-brain-proposal-contract .callout-definition title="The proposal record"}

***The Proposal Record***\index{Proposal Record!definition}\index{Proposal contract!definition}\index{Proposal boundary!contract schema} ($\mathcal{P}$) is a typed candidate-motion payload sent from the unprivileged Brain to the real-time Nervous System. The payload illustration here packages candidate trajectory setpoints, capture timestamps, evidence validity horizons, and provenance metadata for independent verification before execution permission is granted:
$$\mathcal{P} = \langle t_{\text{capture}}, t_{\text{valid}}, H, \Delta t, \mathbf{Q}_{1:H}, \dot{\mathbf{Q}}_{1:H}, \mathbf{X}_{1:H}, \mathbf{g}_{1:H}, \text{model\_id}, \text{lease\_id}, \hat{p}, \text{crc} \rangle$$

1. **Significance**: By formalizing candidate motion into an explicit contract with capture timestamps and validity bounds, the Nervous System can reject stale or uncalibrated proposals before any setpoint reaches an actuator.
2. **Distinction**: Unlike an internal neural tensor, the Proposal Record is an immutable, verifiable boundary payload checked against physical invariant envelopes.
3. **Common pitfall**: Omitting observation timestamps or validity horizons, causing downstream controllers to execute delayed proposals computed from obsolete scene states.

:::

The fields in @tbl-03-proposal-record-schema illustrate what the receiver needs to interpret a candidate trajectory. The trajectory and its observation time come from the proposer; the header and handoff contract in the Nervous System determine how the receiver checks delivery and expiration. The payload describes requested motion; the handoff record establishes the conditions under which that request may reach the body.

| Field         | Type                        | Unit                    | Systems Semantics and Verification Rule                                                                            |
|:--------------|:----------------------------|:------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `t_capture`   | `uint64_t`                  | $\text{ns}$             | Hardware timestamp of oldest sensory observation conditioning the proposal.                                        |
| `t_valid`     | `uint64_t`                  | $\text{ns}$             | Monotonic time after which proposal expires ($\le t_{\text{capture}} + \tau_{\text{ev}}$).                         |
| `horizon_H`   | `uint16_t`                  | count                   | Number of prospective trajectory setpoints ($H = 16\text{--}64$).                                                  |
| `delta_t`     | `uint32_t`                  | $\mu\text{s}$           | Temporal interval between consecutive waypoints ($\Delta t = 20\,000\,\mu\text{s} \implies 50\text{ Hz}$).         |
| `q_traj`      | `float32[H][D]`             | $\text{rad}$            | Candidate joint trajectory array across $D$ degrees of freedom.                                                    |
| `q_dot_traj`  | `float32[H][D]`             | $\text{rad/s}$          | Velocity setpoints; checked for continuity when adjoining chunks meet.                                             |
| `x_cartesian` | `position + orientation[H]` | $\text{m}, \text{quat}$ | End-effector target poses; verified against workspace keep-out boundaries.                                         |
| `gripper_cmd` | `float32[H]`                | $[0, 1]$                | Gripper closure target; evaluated against grasp force and slip limits.                                             |
| `model_id`    | `uint32_t`                  | identifier              | Identifier resolving to the model architecture, weights checkpoint, and calibration profile.                       |
| `confidence`  | `float32`                   | $[0, 1]$                | Model reported confidence $\hat{p}$; interpreted using calibration evidence from observed outcomes.                |
| `lease_id`    | `uint64_t`                  | identifier              | Identifier linking the proposal to a time-limited permission record; the handoff protocol follows in @sec-nervous. |
| `crc32`       | `uint32_t`                  | checksum                | Integrity checksum protecting shared-memory ring buffer payload.                                                   |

: **The formal Proposal Record schema**: Data contract emitted across the proposal boundary from the unprivileged Brain to the real-time Nervous System. {#tbl-03-proposal-record-schema tbl-colwidths="[18,14,14,54]"}

↪ Zero-copy proposal passing between the Brain and the Nervous System relies on the lock-free buffers analyzed in @sec-nervous-cadences.
:::

   Proposals reach the permission path through the handoff of @sec-nervous, and the permission path can refuse a hallucinated proposal when independent measurements, modeled limits, and a feasible fallback support that decision.[^fn-math-unprivileged-control]

[^fn-math-unprivileged-control]: **Proposal Boundary**\index{Proposal boundary!unprivileged proposals}: Treating the neural policy as an unprivileged proposal generator isolates stochastic inference from actuator registers. Candidate trajectory setpoints $\mathbf{q}_{\text{ref}}(t)$ are checked on dedicated safety silicon, so proposals that violate modeled actuator limits or keep-out regions can be rejected before any reaches a drive (@sec-nervous-actuation-authority).

::: {#fig-vln-navigation fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Topological vision-language navigation**: Embodied navigation architecture executing natural-language spatial instructions. Panoramic visual observations are encoded into perceptual tokens, matched against prompt embeddings, and cross-referenced with a dynamically updated topological navigation graph. The action decoder prunes unreachable nodes and emits metric waypoint offsets $(\Delta x, \Delta y)$ and heading setpoints to guide the chassis along traversable semantic frontiers without requiring an exact geometric prior map. (Adapted from An et al. [@an2023etpnav])." fig-alt="Schematic of topological vision-language navigation showing panoramic observation tokens, topological graph matching, and decoded waypoint offsets and heading setpoints."}
![](images/png/fig03_real_vln_topological_navigation.png){width="95%"}
:::

Each neural stage of this pipeline is paid for in memory traffic. Every patch token must be attended over and held in the KV cache, and every evaluation of the backbone streams its weights from DRAM, so the capabilities this section described arrive at a rate the application processor sets rather than one the task chooses. On the mobile manipulator, that rate for its largest model falls well below the rate at which its arm consumes setpoints.

## Supply, Freshness, and the Memory Wall {#sec-brain-cognitive-pipeline}

At the pick station the mobile manipulator's arm consumes a new setpoint every few tens of milliseconds, while the mug it is reaching for keeps moving along the conveyor. Whatever model proposes those setpoints must settle two questions. The first is how often it can produce a proposal on the application processor the machine actually has; the second is how long each proposal stays true once the mug has moved. The answers explain why the machine carries two learned proposers rather than one.

After ingestion (the tokenization of @sec-brain-learned-representations), four stages turn those tokens into proposals (@fig-cognitive-pipeline), and Part III develops each one. Here they matter only for what each hands downstream and how quickly that goes stale.

On an edge robotics SoC operating with a **Unified Memory Architecture (UMA)**—such as an onboard NVIDIA Jetson Orin or Thor compute module—physical memory bandwidth is a shared zero-sum resource. The CPU host cores, GPU/NPU matrix execution units, Image Signal Processors (ISPs), and DMA controllers all share a single physical LPDDR5 bus ($B_{\text{mem}} \approx 204\,\text{GB/s}$). Saturating this bus with gigabytes of neural weight streaming creates direct real-time safety hazards: when a multi-billion-parameter foundation model consumes 90 percent of memory bus cycles, incoming high-bandwidth sensor streams (such as raw MIPI-CSI camera video and Ethernet LiDAR packets) suffer memory controller arbitration stalls. Internal hardware FIFO buffers overflow, dropping frames and blinding perception precisely while the machine is in motion.

Perception grounds what it recognizes in metric coordinates relative to the base, so that the mug becomes an $SE(3)$ pose and a graspable handle rather than an abstract semantic label;[^fn-brain-metric-grounding] its output ages from the moment of capture, and @sec-perception turns that age into a contract. Memory carries those estimates through occlusion and must let each one expire when the evidence behind it does (@sec-memory). Intent decomposes a task such as "take the ceramic mug off the conveyor and hand it to the coworker at the packing station" into subgoals, and because the mug moves while the intent model deliberates, it hands the planner a target that expires, an intent lease\index{Intent lease!temporal contract} (@sec-intent-lease). Planning converts that target into candidate setpoints for the base and the arm, the proposals the permission path will judge (@sec-planning). These stages, and the ingestion before them, all run on the application processor and draw on the same memory bus, which is where the machine's cadence is decided.

[^fn-brain-metric-grounding]: **Metric Spatial Grounding**\index{Metric spatial grounding}\index{Special Euclidean group!SE(3) grounding}: While disembodied AI operates over discrete semantic tokens, physical AI must ground those semantics in the Special Euclidean group $SE(3)$, mapping entities to metric distances (meters) and spatial orientations (quaternions) relative to the robot's base coordinate frame. Failing to maintain this metric grounding causes neural policies to emit kinematically impossible Cartesian paths that breach actuator workspace boundaries.

::: {#fig-cognitive-pipeline fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**The physical AI cognitive flow**: Information flows sequentially from physical sensors through Ingestion (tokenization), Perception (spatial geometry and affordances), Memory (persistent world model belief), Intent (deliberative goal leases), and Planning (multi-step action chunking). The flow ends at the proposal boundary, where the permission path evaluates each proposed action against real-time constraints and resources." fig-alt="Horizontal flowchart of the five-stage cognitive pipeline: Ingestion, Perception, Memory, Intent, and Planning, culminating at the proposal boundary."}
![](images/svg/fig03_cognitive_pipeline_horizontal.svg){width="95%"}
:::

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ High-throughput neural inference accelerators are isolated from deterministic cores in @sec-placement-two-paths-one-die.
:::

### The memory wall {#sec-brain-memory-wall}

When each evaluation streams weights that cannot remain on-chip, memory bandwidth can limit the update cadence of an embodied neural policy even when arithmetic capacity is available. In high-performance computing, the **memory wall**\index{Memory wall!physical inference} defines the operational regime where computational execution units spend the vast majority of clock cycles stalled, waiting for operands to arrive from external memory. In physical AI, this architectural bottleneck is exacerbated by the strict real-time requirement to interact continuously with physical mass: while modern edge accelerator silicon delivers hundreds of teraflops of matrix multiplication performance, the physical interconnect pins and memory interfaces between the processor die and off-chip memory packages provide comparatively modest data transfer rates.

On an edge SoC, the memory hierarchy features a stark bandwidth and latency asymmetry:

* **On-Chip SRAM and System-Level Cache (SLC):** Integrated directly onto the silicon die, local SRAM banks and shared SLC deliver massive sustained bandwidth ($> 1.5\text{--}3.0\,\text{TB/s}$) with ultra-low access latency ($< 1\text{--}10\,\text{ns}$). However, physical die-area constraints and static leakage current limit on-chip capacity to tens of megabytes ($32\text{--}64\,\text{MB}$).
* **Off-Chip LPDDR5 DRAM:** External DRAM packages store tens of gigabytes ($32\text{--}64\,\text{GB}$) required to hold multi-billion-parameter model weights, but data must travel across external printed circuit board (PCB) traces and package pins. Sustained transfer bandwidth is throttled to $140\text{--}204\,\text{GB/s}$, and memory controller access latency climbs to $80\text{--}120\,\text{ns}$.

To understand the physical consequence of this bandwidth ceiling, consider what happens if a robot attempts to generate continuous motor actions one discrete step at a time through an autoregressive foundation model (such as a multi-billion-parameter VLA model). For a decoder that revisits nonresident weights at each token step, each evaluation streams those weights across the external DRAM bus. In single-token decoding with request batch size $B = 1$, the dense weight projections become matrix-vector operations ($\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}$), yielding an arithmetic intensity of just $I \approx 1.0\,\text{FLOP/byte}$. The sustained memory bandwidth $B_{\text{mem}}$ and model weight footprint $M_{\text{weights}}$ strictly bound the maximum fresh-evaluation frequency:
$$f \le \frac{B_{\text{mem}}}{M_{\text{weights}}}$$
Even on flagship edge accelerators equipped with wide LPDDR5 interfaces ($B_{\text{mem}} \approx 140\text{--}204\,\text{GB/s}$ sustained)—such as Jetson Orin or Thor SoCs—executing quantized or compact 3B–7B policies ($M_{\text{weights}} \approx 4.6\text{--}14\,\text{GB}$), this bandwidth ceiling caps inference cadence at:
$$f \le \frac{B_{\text{mem}}}{M_{\text{weights}}} \approx 10\text{--}44\,\text{Hz}$$
before tokenization, multimodal attention, or decoding adds any latency. In single-step autoregressive generation, each action dimension requires predicting additional tokens; if each token revisits off-chip parameters, latency scales linearly with degrees of freedom. Because physical stabilization, joint impedance control, and reflex-level collision avoidance require deterministic update rates of $100\text{--}1000\,\text{Hz}$, **foundation models cannot serve as executive controllers in real-time physical loops**. They are physically trapped behind the memory wall, mathematically forcing an architecture where foundation models operate solely as unprivileged proposal engines.

Deconstructing the complete end-to-end latency budget underscores this architectural partition:
$$\text{Latency}_{\text{E2E}} = t_{\text{shutter}} + t_{\text{MIPI-DMA}} + t_{\text{vision-encoder}} + t_{\text{policy-backbone}} + t_{\text{action-decoder}} + t_{\text{detokenize}} + t_{\text{CAN-bus}} + t_{\text{FOC-driver}}$$
Where camera shutter exposure integration requires $t_{\text{shutter}} \approx 10\text{--}33\,\text{ms}$, serial MIPI CSI-2 DMA frame grab adds $t_{\text{MIPI-DMA}} \approx 1\text{--}2\,\text{ms}$, Vision Transformer feature extraction takes $t_{\text{vision-encoder}} \approx 15\text{--}30\,\text{ms}$, policy backbone evaluation takes $t_{\text{policy-backbone}} \approx 30\text{--}80\,\text{ms}$, action chunk decoding consumes $t_{\text{action-decoder}} \approx 5\text{--}15\,\text{ms}$, action de-tokenization and safety validation takes $t_{\text{detokenize}} \approx 0.5\text{--}1.0\,\text{ms}$, CAN bus transmission adds $t_{\text{CAN-bus}} \approx 0.5\text{--}2.0\,\text{ms}$, and motor driver current control takes $t_{\text{FOC-driver}} \approx 0.05\text{--}0.1\,\text{ms}$, total latency reaches $60\text{--}160\,\text{ms}$. For detailed memory wall derivations and roofline hardware models, see @sec-appendix-systems.

This memory wall[^fn-hw-dram-bandwidth] places single-token streaming deep in the memory-bound region of the roofline (@fig-patterson-roofline) [@williams2009roofline]. On the mobile manipulator's application processor it caps the intent model's fresh-evaluation rate, before any vision or decoding work, far below the rate of a joint controller that asks for a new command every millisecond (\ref{nbk-brain-lpddr5-memory-wall-bottleneck-action-chunking}). A model renewed that slowly can say where the arm should go, but it cannot close the loop on moving mass, so it proposes waypoints and a faster loop below it tracks them.

[Single-token decoding at batch size 1]{.heading-3-inline}
Servers can combine independent requests so that a weight matrix multiplies several input vectors at once, reusing fetched weights. A robot waiting for its next action token often has only one such request. Waiting for future observations to form a batch would add delay, and sequentially dependent action tokens cannot all be evaluated at once by an autoregressive decoder. This limits reuse in those projections. It does not make every operation in an embodied model a matrix-vector product. Image patches, multiple camera views, prompt tokens, and parallel action decoders can expose matrix-matrix work within one robot's request. The low-intensity estimate therefore describes the single-token weight sweep, not the complete perception-and-action workload.

[^fn-hw-dram-bandwidth]: **Autoregressive DRAM Bandwidth Saturation**\index{GPU!memory bandwidth wall}: Sequential action tokens can trigger repeated full-model weight traffic when weights are nonresident and the decoder revisits the backbone; cache behavior and hardware determine the actual bandwidth ceiling. Action chunking is one way to reduce the number of full policy evaluations per unit of physical time.

This continuous data movement also carries an energy penalty. Fetching weights from off-chip DRAM consumes orders of magnitude more energy than the arithmetic computation itself ($\approx 10\text{--}20\,\text{pJ/bit}$, or $80\text{--}160\,\text{pJ/byte}$ for LPDDR5 DRAM access versus $< 0.1\,\text{pJ/FLOP}$ for on-chip FP16 multiply-accumulate). Sweeping a 14 GB model footprint across DRAM dissipates over 1.1 to 2.2 Joules per forward pass purely in memory I/O, generating 11 to 22 Watts of continuous thermal dissipation at a 10 Hz inference cadence. That continuous memory traffic drains battery reserves, and the heat it leaves in the chassis raises the local ambient temperature of the joint actuators, shrinking the thermal winding margins codified in @sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles.

::: {#fig-patterson-roofline fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Illustrative embodied roofline**: Arithmetic intensity against attainable throughput for an example edge accelerator. Single-token weight streaming can be memory-bound. Chunk length alone does not determine arithmetic intensity; chunked workloads require measured operations and memory traffic. A separate real-time loop executes accepted waypoints between fresh model updates." fig-alt="Illustrative roofline diagram plotting arithmetic intensity against attainable throughput, with a single-token weight-streaming point and a ridge separating memory and compute bounds."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ EMBODIED ROOFLINE (FIGURE)
# │ Context: @fig-patterson-roofline
# │ Goal:    show that embodied inference sits far inside the memory-bound regime
# │ Show:    arithmetic intensity against attainable throughput for an edge part
# │ How:     roof from the registry node; the point represents an FP16
# │          matrix-vector weight sweep, excluding other memory traffic
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim import Embodied

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

# ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────────
node = RM.brain_soc  # category: datasheet; the mobile manipulator's application processor
I_TOKEN = 1.0  # category: illustrative; FLOP/byte for a single-token weight sweep

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
peak = node.compute.peak_flops.to("TFLOPs/s").magnitude
bw = node.memory.bandwidth.to("GB/s").magnitude
ridge = peak / (bw / 1000)  # FLOP/byte
attainable = lambda ai: min(bw * ai / 1000, peak)

points = [
    ("Autoregressive VLA\n(single token)", I_TOKEN),
]

# ┌── 3. PLOT ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, ax = viz.plot_roofline(node)
COLORS = viz.COLORS
ax.set_ylim(peak * 0.0004, peak * 2)  # keep the single-token point on scale
for idx, (label, ai) in enumerate(points):
    y = attainable(ai)
    ax.plot(ai, y, "o", ms=8, color=COLORS["VioletLine"], zorder=11)
    # the lowest point has no room beneath the roof, so its label goes above
    if idx == 0:
        pos, ha, va = (ai * 0.30, y * 4.0), "left", "bottom"
    else:
        pos, ha, va = (ai * 2.4, y * 0.30), "left", "top"
    ax.annotate(
        label,
        xy=(ai, y),
        xytext=pos,
        fontsize=8,
        color=COLORS["VioletLine"],
        ha=ha,
        va=va,
        zorder=11,
        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS["VioletLine"], lw=0.9),
    )

# the reuse a workload would need before it left the memory-bound regime
ax.annotate(
    f"intensity must reach {ridge:.0f} FLOP/byte\nbefore compute binds",
    xy=(ridge, peak * 0.006),
    xytext=(ridge * 0.30, peak * 0.0012),
    fontsize=8,
    color=COLORS["primary"],
    ha="right",
    zorder=11,
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS["primary"], lw=0.9),
)
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

The roofline model in @fig-patterson-roofline formalizes the hardware boundary governing embodied inference by plotting attainable computational throughput against **arithmetic intensity** ($I$), defined as:
$$I = \frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{Bytes transferred from off-chip memory}}$$
Consider the dense weight projections in single-token autoregressive decoding at batch size 1, each evaluating a matrix-vector product $\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}$. Counting weight traffic alone, with each weight fetched once for that projection, gives an optimistic intensity estimate; activation and context traffic add further bytes. In 16-bit floating-point precision (FP16, 2 bytes per parameter), each weight participates in exactly one multiply-accumulate operation (2 FLOPs), yielding an arithmetic intensity of:
$$I_{\text{token}} = \frac{2\,\text{FLOPs}}{2\,\text{Bytes}} = 1.0\,\text{FLOP/byte}$$
On the mobile manipulator's application processor (`node = RM.brain_soc`, an edge SoC with $\Pi_{\text{peak}} = 275\,\text{TFLOPs/s}$ FP16 compute and $\beta_{\text{mem}} = 204\,\text{GB/s}$ memory bandwidth), the hardware ridge point occurs at:
$$I_{\text{ridge}} = \frac{\Pi_{\text{peak}}}{\beta_{\text{mem}}} = \frac{275 \times 10^{12}\,\text{FLOPs/s}}{204 \times 10^9\,\text{Bytes/s}} \approx 1348\,\text{FLOP/byte}$$
For this weight-streaming example, $I_{\text{token}} = 1.0\,\text{FLOP/byte} \ll I_{\text{ridge}} \approx 1348\,\text{FLOP/byte}$, so memory bandwidth sets the roofline ceiling. Attainable throughput is bounded by $\beta_{\text{mem}} \cdot I_{\text{token}} \approx 0.204\,\text{TFLOPs/s}$, less than 0.1 percent of peak arithmetic throughput. That ratio is a workload throughput bound, not a measurement of how many cores are idle. If a 7-billion-parameter FP16 decoder emits a 7-DoF action through seven sequential tokens and rereads all weights for each token, the seven transfers alone require nearly $500\,\text{ms}$ at the stated bandwidth. A controller that waits for that entire sequence before each motor update would miss a millisecond deadline; a separate tracking loop must continue between policy evaluations.

Action chunking reduces backbone weight traffic per supplied waypoint when one backbone evaluation supports several future actions. That amortization does not establish an equal increase in arithmetic intensity. Predicting a chunk can add decoder work without repeating the backbone's matrix operations for every waypoint; its roofline position depends on the operations performed and the bytes actually transferred.

For an iterative decoder, each refinement pass adds work on the action head. If the head's weights and intermediate state remain resident on chip, later passes can reuse them without another off-chip transfer. If they do not fit, those passes also add memory traffic. Neither the chunk length nor the number of refinement passes alone determines the whole policy's intensity or attainable throughput. The backbone and head must first be budgeted separately, then combined over the same evaluation interval.

### Action chunking {#sec-brain-action-chunking}

The memory bound limits how often a large model can revise its proposal. A controller can track previously admitted motion between those revisions, but a policy that supplies only one future setpoint leaves little planned motion available while it computes. Predicting a trajectory segment gives the controller a sequence to track without making the next fresh observation arrive sooner.

[Supply rate vs. closed-loop reaction latency]{.heading-3-inline}
To supply dense waypoints despite slow full-model inference, modern physical AI policies employ **action chunking**\index{Action chunking!temporal trajectory} (\ref{dfn-brain-action-chunking}) [@zhao2023learning; @chi2024diffusionpolicy]. Each chunk then crosses the proposal boundary as one packet, the chunk payload of @sec-nervous-cadences. The transfer saving follows from reusing one evaluation across several outputs.

Predicting a horizon of $H \in [8, 64]$ actions per forward pass spreads the multi-gigabyte DRAM weight streaming cost over $H \times \Delta t_{\text{step}}$ seconds of physical execution. On an edge SoC with $B_{\text{mem}} \approx 204\,\text{GB/s}$ running a 7B FP16 model ($14\,\text{GB}$), generating single-step actions at $50\,\text{Hz}$ would demand $50 \times 14\,\text{GB} = 700\,\text{GB/s}$ of sustained memory bandwidth—exceeding physical bus capacity by over $3.4\times$. An action chunk of $H = 16$ waypoints reduces demanded bandwidth by sixteenfold to $700 / 16 \approx 43.8\,\text{GB/s}$ if one such sweep supplies each full chunk. More frequent replanning, decoder work, and competing memory traffic consume additional bandwidth.

Predicting a sequence also changes how a learned policy uses recent actions, but chunking alone does not establish that the policy attends to the right evidence or recovers from an unfamiliar contact. Those properties depend on training and closed-loop evaluation. The supply calculation establishes only the weight traffic needed for the stated execution schedule.

However, systems engineers must never confuse **setpoint supply cadence** with **closed-loop reaction bandwidth**:

* *Setpoint supply cadence* ($f_{\text{supply}} = 1/\Delta t_{\text{step}} = 50\,\text{Hz}$): The rate at which the trajectory queue delivers discrete waypoints to the joint servo loop.
* *Policy replanning rate* ($f_{\text{replan}} = 20\,\text{Hz}$, period $T_{\text{replan}} = 50\,\text{ms}$): The cadence at which the neural backbone evaluates new sensory frames.
* *Closed-loop reaction latency* ($T_{\text{reaction}} = T_{\text{replan}} + t_{\text{infer}} = 50\,\text{ms} + 40\,\text{ms} = 90\,\text{ms}$): The true physical delay before an unmodeled external disturbance or obstacle perceived by the camera can alter the proposed path.

Action chunking solves actuator starvation (supply rate), not feedback latency. If an unexpected obstacle appears immediately after camera exposure, the robot continues executing the open-loop chunk for up to $90\,\text{ms}$ before a revised proposal arrives. Disturbance rejection and obstacle compliance cannot rely on chunk policies; they must be guaranteed by the 1 kHz real-time Nervous System.

A chunking policy (such as Action Chunking with Transformers [ACT], Diffusion Policy, or Flow Matching) generates its whole chunk of $H$ setpoints in one backbone pass followed, for an iterative decoder, by $K = 10\text{--}16$ refinement steps.

An iterative decoder refines a candidate trajectory over several passes. Generative decoders can represent alternative routes around an obstacle, whereas direct mean-squared-error regression can average those routes into an unusable path. @Sec-appendix-ml-diffusion derives the noise-prediction and flow-matching objectives. For the runtime budget here, the decisive quantities are the number of refinement passes, the working set each pass touches, and whether refinement reevaluates the large backbone.

In the separated backbone-and-head design considered here, the $K$ iterative refinement steps run **on the compact action head** (typically a $\sim 50\text{M}$-parameter temporal 1D-U-Net or lightweight multilayer perceptron (MLP) or transformer decoder), **without reevaluating the 7-billion-parameter foundation model backbone**. The 7B vision-language backbone executes only once per replanning cycle to extract $\mathbf{h}_{\text{context}}$, streaming its multi-gigabyte weight footprint across off-chip DRAM once every $50\text{--}200\,\text{ms}$.

Because the 50M action head occupies under $100\,\text{MB}$ in FP16 (or $\approx 25\,\text{MB}$ in INT4), cache residency must be checked against the space available for both parameters and intermediate activation tensors. A compact parameter count alone does not establish residency in on-chip SRAM or system-level cache (SLC). When that working set remains resident, the $K$ refinement passes can use on-chip bandwidth ($> 1.5\text{--}3.0\,\text{TB/s}$ SRAM bandwidth) without repeatedly saturating the off-chip DRAM bus ($204\,\text{GB/s}$). Furthermore, executing $K = 10\text{--}16$ iterative steps in standard eager-mode frameworks would dispatch hundreds of small layer kernels, incurring catastrophic **kernel launch overhead** ($\approx 5\text{--}15\,\mu\text{s}$ CPU-to-GPU launch latency per kernel) that serializes execution on host dispatch queues. Embodied runtimes can reduce repeated CPU dispatch overhead via **CUDA Graph capture** or compiled execution graphs (such as TensorRT engines or TorchDynamo ahead-of-time (AOT) compilation), executing the entire iterative denoising loop as a single hardware-scheduled task on device in $5\text{--}15\,\text{ms}$.

Reducing the number of refinement steps can reduce decoder latency, provided the resulting proposals retain the required task quality. That trade-off needs measurement for the selected policy and processor. It does not remove the time required to encode a fresh observation or evaluate the backbone.

::: {#dfn-brain-action-chunking .callout-definition title="Temporal action chunking"}

***Temporal action chunking***\index{Temporal action chunking!definition}\index{Action chunking!definition} is the policy formulation that predicts an entire horizon of $H$ future continuous actions $\mathbf{A}_{t:t+H-1} = [\mathbf{a}_t, \dots, \mathbf{a}_{t+H-1}]$ in a single neural evaluation or diffusion rollout, amortizing parameter memory transfers across extended physical execution windows.

1.  **Significance**: On a bandwidth-limited device, repeating a full model evaluation for every action can be too slow for millisecond control. Temporal action chunking can reuse a backbone evaluation across multiple waypoints; it does not make fresh observations or policy decisions arrive at the waypoint rate. A downstream controller tracks the accepted trajectory between model updates.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike single-step Markovian policies $\mathbf{a}_t \sim \pi(\cdot \mid \mathbf{o}_t)$ that re-evaluate the full neural network at every control step, action chunking deliberately generates multi-step feedforward trajectories, utilizing receding-horizon execution and blending across overlapping chunks to reconcile slow neural deliberation with fast closed-loop control.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Executing action chunks open-loop without continuous temporal smoothing or runtime safety filtering. Without smooth blending across overlapping chunk boundaries, switching between independently generated horizons injects acceleration jumps and torque shocks that excite mechanical gearbox resonances.

:::
For example, when a canonical bimanual manipulator threads a flexible USB cable (@fig-aloha-manipulator), it executes a 32-step action chunk, a longer chunk than the mobile manipulator uses. The policy emits coordinated 14-DoF joint setpoints that smoothly align both grippers, flex the cable, and insert the connector without pausing between individual control cycles.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_action_chunk_windows_strip.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Sequence strip illustrating overlapping action chunk horizons of 32 steps with 12-step replanning and temporal ensembling."}

*Overlapping action chunks blend predictions across receding temporal execution windows.*
:::

However, action chunking introduces the problem of **chunk seam continuity**. Because each action chunk is generated independently from rolling sensory observations, the tail of chunk $k$ and the head of chunk $k+1$ may exhibit slight positional and velocity discrepancies. If a controller concatenated these chunks directly, the resulting step-discontinuities in acceleration would inject large jerk ($\dddot{\mathbf{q}}$) into the physical linkages, inducing mechanical shock, acoustic vibration, cycloidal pin wear, and motor overcurrent faults.

To reduce discontinuities between overlapping chunks, systems can implement **temporal ensembling**\index{Temporal ensembling!trajectory smoothing}, blending overlapping trajectory predictions via exponentially weighted averaging:

$$\mathbf{a}_t = \frac{\sum_{i=0}^{\min(t, H-1)} w_i \, \mathbf{a}_{t \mid t-i}}{\sum_{i=0}^{\min(t, H-1)} w_i}, \quad w_i = \exp(-m \cdot i)$$

where $\mathbf{a}_{t \mid t-i}$ represents the action predicted for time step $t$ by the action chunk initiated at time $t-i$, and $m > 0$ is a tunable temporal discount factor. The permission path interpolates the blended waypoints below the proposal boundary (@sec-nervous-cadences).

::: {.callout-perspective title="The temporal ensembling jerk trap"}
Exponentially weighted temporal ensembling averages overlapping predictions, but averaging sampled setpoints alone guarantees neither continuous position nor continuous velocity between samples or at chunk boundaries. A downstream interpolator determines those properties. If successive chunks disagree in slope, a controller can receive a step in commanded velocity even when position remains continuous. In joint PD tracking ($\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{K}_p \mathbf{e} + \mathbf{K}_d \dot{\mathbf{e}}$), that velocity jump produces a finite torque step. With derivative gain $K_d = 40\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}\cdot\text{s/rad}$ and velocity discontinuity $\Delta \dot{q} = 0.5\,\text{rad/s}$, the derivative term changes by $\Delta \tau = K_d \Delta \dot{q} = 20\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$. Dividing by the servo period would instead describe a torque slew rate, not a torque. Abrupt torque changes can excite mechanical resonances or exceed drive limits. Interpolation must match position, velocity, and acceleration at adjoining segments to provide $C^2$ continuity, while enforcing the machine's velocity, acceleration, and torque limits. Smoothness alone does not establish that the requested motion is feasible.
:::

The separation between policy renewal and trajectory tracking determines what an action rate means (@fig-03-vla-scaling-timeline). Discrete decoders generate action tokens sequentially [@brohan2023rt1; @brohan2023rt2; @kim2024openvla]. Chunked decoders generate several candidate waypoints from one sensory context, either directly or through iterative refinement [@zhao2023learning; @chi2024diffusionpolicy; @black2024pi0]. Supplying more waypoints from that context does not refresh the observation on which they depend.

A downstream controller can use current state measurements while tracking admitted waypoints between policy renewals. Its feedback corrects tracking errors within its capabilities; a newly perceived obstacle still requires a timely checking or replanning response. The worked mobile-manipulator budget below therefore distinguishes the interval between fresh policy evaluations from the spacing between waypoints.

::: {#fig-03-vla-scaling-timeline fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Policy renewal and trajectory tracking**: Each fresh policy evaluation produces candidate motion from a sensory context. Overlapping chunks can supply waypoints between renewals, while a downstream controller uses current state feedback to track admitted motion. Additional waypoints do not refresh the policy's evidence. This schematic shows timing relationships, not measured rates or a hardware performance comparison." fig-alt="Three timing rows distinguish fresh observation and policy evaluation events, overlapping candidate chunks, and frequent downstream tracking steps with current state feedback. The shared time axis has no numerical scale."}

```{python}
#| label: fig-03-vla-scaling-timeline
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ POLICY RENEWAL AND TRAJECTORY TRACKING (SCHEMATIC)
# │ Context: @fig-03-vla-scaling-timeline
# │ Goal:    distinguish renewed evidence from supplied waypoints and feedback
# │ Show:    temporal ordering only; coordinates are layout, not measured data
# │ How:     separate observation, chunk, and downstream tracking rows
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import viz
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle

fig, ax, _, _ = viz.setup_plot(figsize=(10, 4.5))
C = viz.COLORS
ax.set_xlim(-3.0, 10.5)
ax.set_ylim(-0.7, 3.4)
ax.axis("off")

rows = [
    (2.6, "Fresh observation\n+ policy evaluation"),
    (1.5, "Candidate chunks\n(subject to permission)"),
    (0.2, "Downstream tracking\n+ current state feedback"),
]
for y, label in rows:
    ax.text(-0.35, y, label, ha="right", va="center", fontsize=9, color=C["primary"])

for x, chunk_y in [(0.3, 1.75), (4.1, 1.40), (7.9, 1.05)]:
    ax.plot(x, 2.6, "o", color=C["BlueLine"], ms=7)
    ax.annotate("", xy=(x + 0.5, chunk_y + 0.14), xytext=(x, 2.48), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=C["primary"], lw=1))

for x, y, end in [(0.8, 1.75, 5.2), (4.6, 1.40, 9.0), (8.4, 1.05, 10.0)]:
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x, y - 0.10), end - x, 0.20, facecolor=C["VioletL"], edgecolor=C["VioletLine"], lw=1))
    for j in range(1, int((end - x) / 0.4)):
        xx = x + j * 0.4
        ax.plot([xx, xx], [y - 0.10, y + 0.10], color=C["VioletLine"], lw=0.7)

for j in range(24):
    x = 0.8 + j * 0.4
    ax.plot([x, x], [0.08, 0.32], color=C["GreenLine"], lw=1.3)
ax.annotate("", xy=(10.1, -0.2), xytext=(0.0, -0.2), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=C["primary"], lw=1))
ax.text(10.1, -0.43, "Physical time (schematic)", ha="right", fontsize=9)
ax.text(5.2, 3.2, "A new waypoint is not a new observation", ha="center", fontsize=11)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::

### Dual proposal pathways in physical inference {#sec-brain-two-proposers}

For the conveyor pick, recognizing the requested object and renewing its motion proposal need not use the same model. The warehouse mobile manipulator assigns task interpretation to a slower intent model and frequent trajectory renewal to a smaller action-chunk policy. Both remain proposers; neither replaces the independent permission path. Notebook \ref{nbk-brain-lpddr5-memory-wall-bottleneck-action-chunking} applies the memory bound to this split and tests whether chunking alone could give the larger model the required renewal cadence.

```{python}
#| label: calc-brain-action-chunking-lpddr5
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ MEMORY WALL AND THE MACHINE'S TWO PROPOSERS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: nbk-brain-lpddr5-memory-wall-bottleneck-action-chunking and the
# │          memory-wall paragraphs that follow it
# │ Goal:    show why the mobile manipulator's intent model cannot renew a
# │          proposal every few tens of milliseconds while its chunk policy can
# │ Show:    98.0 ms per intent-model weight sweep (about 10 Hz before vision);
# │          6.1 ms amortized weight-sweep time per setpoint over H = 16;
# │          0.70 ms per chunk-policy sweep; intent 5 Hz / 160 ms; chunk policy
# │          20 Hz / 40 ms
# │ How:     t_stream = M_weights / (B_peak * dram_efficiency);
# │          tau_step = t_stream / H (calc_action_chunk_streaming_amortization)
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import (
    fmt_params,
    fmt_memory,
    fmt_bandwidth,
    fmt_latency,
    fmt_time,
    fmt_frequency,
    fmt_percent,
    fmt_int,
    fmt_display_math,
    check,
)

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class ActionChunkingLPDDR5:
    """Memory wall and action chunking amortization on the machine's application processor."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    model = RM.intent_model  # category: chosen (the machine's intent model)
    chunk_model = RM.chunk_model  # category: chosen (the machine's chunk policy)
    soc = RM.brain_soc  # category: datasheet (application processor)
    params = model.parameters  # category: datasheet
    chunk_params = chunk_model.parameters  # category: datasheet
    bytes_per_param = 2 * (byte / param)  # category: chosen; FP16 weight storage
    bytes_per_param_int4 = 0.5 * (byte / param)  # category: chosen; INT4 alternative
    b_peak = soc.memory.bandwidth  # category: datasheet
    soc_mem = soc.memory.capacity  # category: datasheet
    bus_efficiency = RM.dram_efficiency  # category: illustrative; sustained fraction of peak
    chunk_horizon = RM.chunk_horizon  # category: chosen
    chunk_step = RM.chunk_step  # category: chosen
    intent_rate = RM.intent_rate  # category: chosen
    intent_latency = RM.intent_inference_latency  # category: illustrative
    chunk_rate = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen
    chunk_latency = RM.chunk_inference_latency  # category: illustrative; P99 incl. vision
    kv_layers = model.layers  # category: datasheet
    kv_hidden = model.hidden_dim  # category: datasheet
    kv_bytes = 2 * byte  # category: chosen; FP16 key and value storage
    cameras = 3  # category: illustrative; synchronized RGB streams
    patches_per_frame = 256  # category: derived; patch tokens per 224 x 224 frame at P = 14
    context_tokens = 800  # category: illustrative; visual plus language and proprioception tokens per step
    history_window = 5 * second  # category: illustrative; retained visual history
    history_rate = 10 * Hz  # category: illustrative; frames retained per second of history

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    weight_mem = memory_from_params(params, bytes_per_param)
    weight_mem_int4 = memory_from_params(params, bytes_per_param_int4)
    res = calc_action_chunk_streaming_amortization(
        model_weight_memory=weight_mem,
        memory_bandwidth=b_peak,
        chunk_horizon=chunk_horizon,
        bus_efficiency=bus_efficiency,
    )
    b_sustained = res["b_sustained"]
    t_stream = res["t_stream"]
    f_single = res["f_single"]
    tau_step = res["tau_step"]
    chunk_span = (chunk_horizon * chunk_step).to(millisecond)

    chunk_weight_mem = memory_from_params(chunk_params, bytes_per_param)
    chunk_res = calc_action_chunk_streaming_amortization(
        model_weight_memory=chunk_weight_mem,
        memory_bandwidth=b_peak,
        chunk_horizon=chunk_horizon,
        bus_efficiency=bus_efficiency,
    )
    chunk_t_stream = chunk_res["t_stream"]

    visual_tokens = cameras * patches_per_frame
    kv_per_token = (2 * kv_layers * kv_hidden * kv_bytes).to(MB)
    kv_per_frame = (kv_per_token * visual_tokens).to(MB)
    history_frames = round((history_window * history_rate).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    kv_history_visual = (kv_per_frame * history_frames).to(GB)
    kv_per_step = (kv_per_token * context_tokens).to(MB)
    kv_history = (kv_per_step * history_frames).to(GB)
    combined_mem = (weight_mem + kv_history).to(GB)
    combined_ratio = (combined_mem / soc_mem).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(weight_mem.to(GB).magnitude - 14.0) < 0.1, f"Unexpected weight footprint: {weight_mem}")
    check(abs(b_sustained.to(GB / second).magnitude - 142.80) < 0.05, f"Unexpected sustained bandwidth: {b_sustained}")
    check(abs(t_stream.to(millisecond).magnitude - 98.04) < 0.005, f"Unexpected intent sweep: {t_stream}")
    check(abs(f_single.magnitude - 10.20) < 0.05, f"Unexpected single-sweep frequency: {f_single}")
    check(chunk_horizon == 16, f"Unexpected chunk horizon: {chunk_horizon}")
    check(abs(tau_step.to(millisecond).magnitude - 6.13) < 0.01, f"Unexpected per-setpoint sweep time: {tau_step}")
    check(abs(chunk_span.magnitude - 320.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected chunk span: {chunk_span}")
    check(abs(chunk_t_stream.to(millisecond).magnitude - 0.700) < 0.0005, f"Unexpected chunk sweep: {chunk_t_stream}")
    check(abs(intent_rate.to(ureg.hertz).magnitude - 5.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected intent rate: {intent_rate}")
    check(abs(intent_latency.to(millisecond).magnitude - 160.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected intent latency: {intent_latency}")
    check(abs(chunk_rate.to(ureg.hertz).magnitude - 20.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected chunk rate: {chunk_rate}")
    check(abs(chunk_latency.to(millisecond).magnitude - 40.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected chunk latency: {chunk_latency}")
    check(t_stream > (1 / chunk_rate), "The intent sweep alone must exceed the chunk period")
    check(chunk_latency < (1 / chunk_rate), "The chunk policy's inference must fit its own period")
    check(kv_layers == 32 and kv_hidden == 4096, f"Unexpected intent-model shape: {kv_layers} x {kv_hidden}")
    check(visual_tokens == 768 and history_frames == 50, f"Unexpected KV scenario: {visual_tokens}, {history_frames}")
    check(abs(kv_per_token.magnitude - 0.524288) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected KV bytes per token: {kv_per_token}")
    check(abs(kv_history_visual.magnitude - 20.13) < 0.01, f"Unexpected visual KV history: {kv_history_visual}")
    check(abs(kv_history.magnitude - 20.97) < 0.01, f"Unexpected context KV history: {kv_history}")
    check(abs(combined_mem.magnitude - 34.97) < 0.01, f"Unexpected weights plus KV footprint: {combined_mem}")
    check(0.45 < combined_ratio < 0.55, f"Weights plus KV must claim about half the SoC memory: {combined_ratio}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    params_str = fmt_params(params, precision=0)
    chunk_params_str = fmt_params(chunk_params, precision=0)
    bytes_per_param_str = fmt_int(bytes_per_param.magnitude)
    weight_mem_str = fmt_memory(weight_mem, unit=GB, precision=0)
    weight_mem_int4_str = fmt_memory(weight_mem_int4, unit=GB, precision=1)
    chunk_weight_mem_str = fmt_memory(chunk_weight_mem, unit=GB, precision=2)
    b_peak_str = fmt_bandwidth(b_peak, unit=GB / second, precision=0)
    b_sustained_str = fmt_bandwidth(b_sustained, unit=GB / second, precision=1)
    dram_eff_pct_str = fmt_percent(bus_efficiency, precision=0)
    t_stream_ms_str = fmt_latency(t_stream, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_stream_s_str = fmt_time(t_stream.to(second), 'second', precision=4)
    f_single_str = fmt_frequency(f_single, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=1)
    chunk_horizon_str = fmt_int(chunk_horizon)
    chunk_step_str = fmt_latency(chunk_step, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    chunk_span_str = fmt_latency(chunk_span, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    tau_step_str = fmt_latency(tau_step, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    chunk_t_stream_str = fmt_latency(chunk_t_stream, unit=millisecond, precision=2)
    intent_rate_str = fmt_frequency(intent_rate, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=0)
    intent_latency_str = fmt_latency(intent_latency, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    chunk_rate_str = fmt_frequency(chunk_rate, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=0)
    chunk_latency_str = fmt_latency(chunk_latency, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    kv_layers_str = fmt_int(kv_layers)
    kv_hidden_str = fmt_int(kv_hidden, commas=False)
    cameras_str = fmt_int(cameras)
    patches_per_frame_str = fmt_int(patches_per_frame)
    visual_tokens_str = fmt_int(visual_tokens)
    context_tokens_str = fmt_int(context_tokens)
    history_window_str = fmt_time(history_window, 'second', precision=0)
    history_rate_str = fmt_frequency(history_rate, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=0)
    kv_per_token_str = fmt_memory(kv_per_token, unit=MB, precision=2)
    kv_per_frame_str = fmt_memory(kv_per_frame, unit=MB, precision=1)
    kv_history_visual_str = fmt_memory(kv_history_visual, unit=GB, precision=1)
    kv_per_step_str = fmt_memory(kv_per_step, unit=MB, precision=1)
    kv_history_str = fmt_memory(kv_history, unit=GB, precision=1)
    combined_mem_str = fmt_memory(combined_mem, unit=GB, precision=1)
    soc_mem_gb_str = fmt_memory(soc_mem, unit=GB, precision=1)

    t_stream_display_math = fmt_display_math(rf"t_{{\text{{stream}}}} = \frac{{{weight_mem_str}}}{{{b_sustained_str}}} \approx {t_stream_ms_str}")
    f_single_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"f_{{\text{{single}}}} = \frac{{1}}{{t_{{\text{{stream}}}}}} \approx \frac{{1}}{{{t_stream_s_str}}} \approx {f_single_str}"
    )
    kv_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"M_{{\text{{KV}}}} = 2 \times L \times d \times S \times \text{{bytes}} = 2 \times {kv_layers_str} \times {kv_hidden_str} \times S \times 2 \approx {kv_per_token_str} \cdot S"
    )
    tau_step_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"\tau_{{\text{{step}}}} = \frac{{t_{{\text{{stream}}}}}}{{H}} = \frac{{{t_stream_ms_str}}}{{{chunk_horizon_str}\text{{ setpoints}}}} \approx {tau_step_str}\text{{ per setpoint}}"
    )
```

::: {#nbk-brain-lpddr5-memory-wall-bottleneck-action-chunking .callout-notebook title="Memory walls, supply, and freshness"}
Can action chunking let a multi-billion-parameter model on an embedded compute module renew proposals as fast as the arm consumes them, or does the machine need a second, smaller proposer?

*1. The single-token memory bottleneck.*
Consider the mobile manipulator's intent model, a `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.params_str` VLA model stored in 16-bit precision (FP16) in the LPDDR5 memory of its application processor, an embedded edge System-on-Chip:

- Weight footprint: $M_{\text{weights}} =$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.params_str` params $\times$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.bytes_per_param_str` bytes $\approx$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.weight_mem_str`.
- Theoretical memory bandwidth: $B_{\text{peak}} =$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.b_peak_str`.
- Assumed sustained DRAM bandwidth (`{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.dram_eff_pct_str` percent of peak to model bus scheduling and memory overhead): $B_{\text{sustained}} \approx$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.b_sustained_str`.

Minimum streaming latency to fetch the weights from DRAM across the silicon bus once:
`{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.t_stream_display_math`

Bandwidth-only upper bound on fresh evaluations when each evaluation streams the full weights:
`{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.f_single_display_math`

Beyond model weights, autoregressive foundation models also grow their KV cache. When multi-camera sensory feeds (e.g., `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.cameras_str` $224 \times 224$ RGB streams) are ingested, each video frame contributes hundreds of visual patch tokens (`{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.cameras_str` $\times$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.patches_per_frame_str` $=$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.visual_tokens_str` tokens). In the intent model's `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.kv_layers_str`-layer transformer with hidden dimension $d =$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.kv_hidden_str`, storing the FP16 Key and Value states consumes `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.kv_per_token_str` per token:
`{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.kv_display_math`
Across a `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.visual_tokens_str`-token visual prompt, the KV cache expands by `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.kv_per_frame_str` per frame.

*2. The action chunking amortization.*
Suppose the intent model itself emitted an action chunk of $H =$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_horizon_str` future setpoints ($\Delta t =$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_step_str`, spanning `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_span_str`) from each forward pass, instead of one action step per DRAM weight sweep.

- Number of weight memory sweeps: 1 sweep (`{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.t_stream_ms_str`).
- A chunk can reuse one backbone evaluation across $H$ future setpoints.
- Amortized weight-sweep time per setpoint (excluding all other inference work):
`{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.tau_step_display_math`

*3. The machine's split.*
Amortization spreads one sweep across more setpoints, but it does not make a fresh proposal arrive sooner. Each new chunk from the intent model would still wait for at least one `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.t_stream_ms_str` sweep, plus tokenization, attention, and decoding. The mobile manipulator therefore divides the work between two models. Its intent model revises the goal at `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.intent_rate_str` with `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.intent_latency_str` of inference. A separate `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_params_str`-parameter chunk policy, whose `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_weight_mem_str` of weights sweep in `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_t_stream_str`, proposes base velocity and arm joint targets together at `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_rate_str` ($50\,\text{ms}$ replanning period), emitting waypoints spaced at $\Delta t =$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_step_str` (a $50\,\text{Hz}$ supply rate), within a `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_latency_str` P99 inference budget that includes vision, while the low-level motor drive interpolates and closes current loops at $10\text{--}25\,\text{kHz}$. The intent model's sweep is too slow to renew a proposal every few tens of milliseconds; the chunk policy's is not. @Sec-nervous turns that difference into a lease.
:::

The `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.t_stream_ms_str` sweep in \ref{nbk-brain-lpddr5-memory-wall-bottleneck-action-chunking} is a floor reached before vision, attention, or decoder work begins. Two alternatives to the machine's split, lower weight precision and a single model with a fast head, would attack it, and neither removes it cheaply. INT4 storage would reduce the nominal weight footprint to `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.weight_mem_int4_str` but needs accuracy validation for contact tasks. A single-model design could instead trade cadence for density without changing weight precision. It would evaluate the `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.params_str` backbone periodically while a lightweight diffusion head denoises candidate trajectories on-chip, supplying dense candidate waypoints from each slower full-model evaluation. Its new-observation rate would still be limited by full inference latency, including vision and decoder work, which is why the mobile manipulator gives renewal to a separate chunk policy instead.

Retained context adds to the pressure the notebook began to measure. Counting language and proprioception tokens along with the visual patches raises each step to $S \approx$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.context_tokens_str` tokens, so at `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.kv_per_token_str` of FP16 key-value state per token each observation step adds `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.kv_per_step_str` of KV cache. Retaining an unpruned `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.history_window_str` historical context window at `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.history_rate_str` yields `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.kv_history_str` of KV cache. Combined with the intent model's `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.weight_mem_str` of weights, this example claims `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.combined_mem_str`, about half of the application processor's `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.soc_mem_gb_str` before runtime overhead, memory that perception, mapping, and the chunk policy also need. Even where memory capacity permits, reading a large cache is further traffic on that same bus (@sec-placement-resource-contention). On edge SoCs utilizing a Unified Memory Architecture, this massive memory traffic has direct safety implications: neural accelerators streaming gigabytes of weights and KV cache saturate the shared memory interconnect. DMA engines transferring incoming camera video streams and LiDAR packets experience memory arbitration stalls, causing dropped sensor frames and perceptual blind spots precisely when the robot is moving. Embodied architectures must therefore avoid unpruned autoregressive visual histories, relying instead on spatial pooling, cross-attention feature projections, or fixed-horizon action chunking.

```{python}
#| label: calc-brain-conveyor-chunk-sizing
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CONVEYOR CHUNK SIZING
```
